96908.e: There are measuring stations on the ground in only a few places and hardly any on the seas. Satellites such as ESA's three Swarm satellites circle the whole Earth.
96908.m: Satellites monitor the Earth's magnetic field worldwide.

96909.q: Which mathematician showed in 1839, using mathematical analysis, that the magnetic field mainly comes from the Earth's interior?
96909.e: Using spherical functions, Gauss split the field into parts coming from inside and outside. An old unit of magnetic flux density is also named after him.
96909.m: Gauss proved that the Earth's magnetic field comes from the Earth's interior.

96910.q: What does a dynamo in the Earth's core need to produce a magnetic field?
96910.e: Flowing liquid iron moves through a magnetic field and induces electric currents. These currents in turn produce the field and keep it going.
96910.m: The geodynamo turns the energy of flow into magnetic energy.

96911.q: Why can a permanent magnet inside the Earth not explain the Earth's magnetic field?
a: It is hotter there than the Curie temperature.
There are no metals in the core.
96911.e: Above the Curie temperature, about 770 °C for iron, substances lose their permanent magnetisation. In the core it is several thousand degrees.
96911.m: A hot Earth core cannot be a permanent magnet.

96912.q: Which force arranges the currents in the outer core into column-like vortices along the axis of rotation?
a: the frictional force of the crust
96912.e: Because the Earth rotates, the rising and sinking currents are deflected sideways. This arranges them in such a way that a large-scale dipole field forms.
96912.m: The Earth's rotation brings order to the currents in the core.

96913.q: Which energy source is mainly driving the geodynamo today?
a: the solidification of the inner core
96913.e: As the inner core grows, heat of crystallisation is released and lighter elements stay behind in the melt. Both make the liquid iron rise and convect.
96913.m: The growing inner core keeps the geodynamo going.

96914.q: What has happened during a reversal of the Earth's magnetic field?
a: The magnetic north and south poles have swapped places
The Earth has rotated the other way round
The magnetic field has disappeared for ever
96914.e: The magnetic field has reversed many times in the Earth's history. Computer models of the geodynamo show that such reversals can happen on their own.
96914.m: The Earth's magnetic field has reversed many times.

96915.q: How do we know that the Earth's outer core is liquid?
a: S waves from earthquakes cannot pass through it
People have drilled down to the core
96915.e: Shear waves (S waves) do not travel through liquids. That is why there is a shadow zone without S waves behind the core. The liquid outer core is over 2000 km thick.
96915.m: Earthquake waves reveal the liquid outer core.

96916.q: Why does Mars no longer have a global magnetic field today?
a: Its core dynamo has died out.
It is too close to the Sun.
96916.e: Magnetised rocks show that Mars used to have a field. Its smaller core cooled faster, and convection came to a halt.
96916.m: Without convection in the core, a planet's magnetic field dies out.

96917.q: What does it mean that the geodynamo sustains itself?
a: The field produces currents, which in turn produce the field
It needs no energy at all
It is driven by the Sun
It consists of a solid magnet
96917.e: Moving liquid iron induces electric currents in the magnetic field. These currents keep rebuilding the magnetic field as long as there is energy for the flow.
96917.m: A self-exciting dynamo keeps its own magnetic field going.

96918.q: How many years ago did the last complete reversal of the Earth's magnetic field take place?
96918.e: Since the Brunhes-Matuyama reversal the field has had its present orientation. It serves geologists as an important time marker.
96918.m: The last pole reversal was about 780,000 years ago.

96919.q: What was the Laschamp event about 41,000 years ago?
a: a short excursion of the magnetic field
the beginning of the last ice age
96919.e: The field weakened greatly and flipped into an almost reversed position for only a few hundred years. After that it returned to its old direction.
96919.m: Not every change in the field leads to a permanent reversal.

96920.q: Which discovery on the seabed supported seafloor spreading in the 1960s?
a: symmetrical magnetic stripes on both sides of the ridges
fossilised forests in the deep seabed
hot springs at the deep-sea trenches
96920.e: In 1963 Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews interpreted the stripes as frozen field directions. New crust records the polarity at the time and is pushed away to both sides.
96920.m: Magnetic stripes on the seabed are a tape recording of the Earth's history.

96921.q: According to current estimates, roughly how long does a pole reversal take?
96921.e: Rock data point to transitions of about 1000 to 10,000 years. During this time the field is weak and irregular.
96921.m: A pole reversal happens in a geologically short time.

96922.q: What is a period of over ten million years in which the magnetic field did not reverse, as in the Cretaceous, called?
96922.e: In the Cretaceous Superchron the field kept the same polarity for about 40 million years. The cause is thought to be changed conditions at the core-mantle boundary.
96922.m: Sometimes the magnetic field stays stable for tens of millions of years.

96923.q: How do volcanic rocks record the direction of the magnetic field at the time they formed?
a: Magnetic minerals line up as they cool.
The crystals always grow towards the south.
The rock takes up iron from water.
96923.e: Minerals such as magnetite take on the direction of the Earth's field when they cool below about 580 °C. This magnetisation is preserved for millions of years (palaeomagnetism).
96923.m: Cooled lava works like a compass from the past.

96924.q: What did the Frenchman Bernard Brunhes discover in lava rock in 1906?
a: Rock that was magnetised against today's magnetic field
The structure of the Earth's core
96924.e: Brunhes studied lava in the French Massif Central. His discovery that the Earth's magnetic field can reverse was doubted for a long time.
96924.m: Brunhes discovered the first traces of reversed magnetic fields.

96925.q: How regularly do pole reversals occur?
a: irregularly, on average every few hundred thousand years
only once in the Earth's history
96925.e: The intervals vary greatly, from less than a hundred thousand to many millions of years. It is therefore not possible to predict the next reversal.
96925.m: Pole reversals do not follow a fixed rhythm.

96926.e: Gravity is not equally strong everywhere. Dense rocks underground increase it slightly, light ones reduce it. It is often measured in milligals.
96926.m: Gravimeters measure tiny differences in gravity.

96927.q: A gravimeter is carried 200 m higher. By how much does g decrease if the free-air gradient is 0.3086 mGal per metre?
96927.e: 200 times 0.3086 mGal gives about 61.7 mGal. That is why the height must be known very precisely when measuring gravity.

96928.q: Why is gravity beneath the Alps lower than you would expect because of the large mass of the mountains?
a: Light crust reaches deep down into the mantle as a root
The ice of the glaciers cancels out gravity
The Earth's core lies deeper beneath the Alps
96928.e: Mountain ranges float on the denser mantle like icebergs (isostasy). The deep crustal root is lighter than the mantle rock that would otherwise be there.
96928.m: Beneath mountains, mass is missing deep down.

96929.q: Which gravity anomaly does an underground salt dome typically produce?
96929.e: At about 2.2 g/cm³, rock salt is lighter than the surrounding sedimentary rock. Gravity above it is therefore slightly lower, which is used when searching for raw materials.

96930.q: How can satellites measure that Greenland is losing ice without seeing the ice?
a: They measure tiny changes in gravity
They count the icebergs in the sea
They listen to the ice cracking
96930.e: Less ice means less mass and therefore slightly less attraction. This is how the GRACE satellites weighed the ice loss in Greenland and Antarctica.
96930.m: Satellites can weigh ice using gravity.

96931.q: What is meant by the geoid?
a: the surface of equal gravitational potential at sea level
the shape of the Earth without mountains
a sphere with the average radius of the Earth
the boundary between crust and mantle
96931.e: The geoid roughly corresponds to the surface of the sea at rest, imagined as continuing beneath the continents. Because masses are unevenly distributed, it differs from the reference ellipsoid by up to about 100 m.
96931.m: The geoid is the shape that seawater at rest would take.

96932.q: Why is the acceleration due to gravity greater at the poles than at the equator?
a: The poles are closer to the centre of the Earth, and there is no centrifugal force.
There is more ice on the Earth at the poles.
The magnetic field increases gravity there.
The air is thinner at the equator.
96932.e: Because the Earth is flattened, the poles are about 21 km closer to its centre. In addition, there is no centrifugal force from the Earth's rotation there, so g is greater, at about 9.83 m/s², than at the equator, at about 9.78 m/s².
96932.m: Flattening and the Earth's rotation make gravity smaller at the equator.

96933.q: How does an absolute gravimeter measure the acceleration due to gravity?
a: with a laser on a freely falling mirror
with a thermometer in a borehole
96933.e: A prism falls in a vacuum chamber, and a laser interferometer measures its position very precisely. From distance and time, g is obtained to within a few billionths.
96933.m: Absolute gravimeters measure free fall with laser light.

96934.q: At the surface it is 10 °C, and the geothermal gradient is 3 °C per 100 m. How warm is it at a depth of 4000 m?
96934.e: 4000 m is 40 times 100 m, so the temperature rises by 40 times 3 °C, which is 120 °C. Adding the 10 °C at the surface gives 130 °C.
96934.m: For geothermal heat at great depth you have to drill deep.

96935.q: Why was the Deep Heat Mining geothermal project in Basel stopped after 2006?
a: It caused earthquakes that could be felt.
96935.e: When water was pumped into hot rock, an earthquake of magnitude 3.4 occurred on 8 December 2006. After a risk analysis, the project was finally abandoned in 2009.
96935.m: Deep geothermal energy can trigger small earthquakes.

96936.q: Where was electricity first produced from geothermal heat, in 1904?
96936.e: In Tuscany, Prince Piero Ginori Conti used steam from the ground to run a generator that lit a few light bulbs. In 1913 the first geothermal power station started operating there.
96936.m: The first geothermal electricity flowed in Tuscany in 1904.

96937.q: Roughly what proportion of buildings in Iceland are heated with geothermal energy?
96937.e: Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and above a hotspot. Hot water is piped into almost all homes through district heating networks.
96937.m: Iceland heats almost entirely with geothermal energy.

96938.q: How deep do ground heat probes for houses in Switzerland typically go?
96938.e: At such depths the rock has an almost constant temperature of about 10 to 15 °C all year round. Switzerland is one of the countries with a particularly large number of ground heat probes.
96938.m: Ground heat probes take heat from a few hundred metres down.

96939.q: Where does the heat inside the Earth mainly come from?
a: From the decay of radioactive elements and heat left over from the Earth's formation
From the friction of the wind
96939.e: About half of the heat flow comes from the decay of uranium, thorium and potassium. The rest is heat that has been stored since the Earth formed.
96939.m: Radioactivity and primordial heat warm the Earth's interior.

96940.q: What distinguishes petrothermal geothermal energy from hydrothermal?
a: Hot, dry rock is used and water is pumped into it.
Only hot springs at the surface are used.
The Sun's heat in the ground is used.
Gas from deep underground is burnt.
96940.e: In hydrothermal geothermal energy, naturally existing hot water is extracted. In petrothermal energy this water is missing, so artificial paths are created in the rock by pumping water in.
96940.m: Petrothermal geothermal energy makes dry, hot rock usable.

96941.q: Why does a heating system with a ground heat probe usually need a heat pump?
a: The water from the probe is too cool for heating.
The probe delivers water that is too hot.
Without a pump the probe would freeze.
The heat pump produces the electricity for the probe.
96941.e: From a few hundred metres down, the liquid comes back at only about 10 °C. The heat pump raises this heat to the temperature needed for heating and hot water.
96941.m: The heat pump makes cool ground heat usable.

96942.q: Which particle acts as a Brønsted acid in the reaction HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₂O?
96942.e: The hydrogen carbonate ion gives a proton to the hydroxide ion and becomes carbonate. The hydroxide ion takes up the proton and becomes water.
96942.m: The acid is the particle that gives off a proton in the reaction.

96943.q: Which particle is the conjugate base of sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄)?
96943.e: The conjugate base forms when the acid gives off exactly one proton. So H₂SO₄ becomes the hydrogen sulphate ion HSO₄⁻.
96943.m: An acid and its conjugate base differ by exactly one proton.

96944.q: Which particle is the conjugate acid of ammonia (NH₃)?
96944.e: When ammonia takes up a proton, the ammonium ion NH₄⁺ forms. This can give the proton off again and is therefore the conjugate acid.
96944.m: When a base takes up a proton, it becomes its conjugate acid.

96945.q: Which chemist formulated the same acid-base theory independently of Brønsted in 1923?
96945.e: The Englishman Thomas Martin Lowry published the concept of proton transfer in 1923, almost at the same time as the Dane Johannes Nicolaus Brønsted. That is why it is often called the Brønsted-Lowry theory.
96945.m: The proton theory of acids bears the names Brønsted and Lowry.

96946.q: Which reaction can be interpreted as an acid-base reaction according to Brønsted, but not according to Arrhenius?
a: NH₃ and HCl react as gases to form solid NH₄Cl
96946.e: Arrhenius related acids and bases to aqueous solutions. In the gas reaction of ammonia with hydrogen chloride, a proton is transferred, so according to Brønsted it is an acid-base reaction, even without water.
96946.m: The Brønsted theory also applies to reactions without water.

96947.q: What role does water play when hydrogen chloride (HCl) dissolves in it?
a: It acts as an oxidising agent
96947.e: HCl gives a proton to a water molecule, forming H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻. The water takes up the proton and is therefore the proton acceptor.
96947.m: When hydrogen chloride dissolves, water takes up a proton.

96948.q: What is a reaction called in which a proton is transferred from one particle to another?
96948.e: A Brønsted acid-base reaction is a proton transfer and is called protolysis. In a redox reaction, by contrast, electrons are transferred.
96948.m: Protolysis is a transfer of protons.

96949.q: In simplified terms, as which particle is a proton described in aqueous solution?
96949.e: A free proton does not exist in water; it immediately attaches to a water molecule. In simplified form this is written H₃O⁺, but in fact it is surrounded by further water molecules.
96949.m: In water, protons are present as oxonium ions.

96950.q: Which country did the chemist Johannes Nicolaus Brønsted come from?
96950.e: Johannes Nicolaus Brønsted (1879 to 1947) was a Danish physical chemist who taught in Copenhagen. The letter ø in his name is typical of Danish.

96951.q: What is the acid dissociation constant Ka for the equilibrium HA + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + A⁻?
96951.e: According to the law of mass action, the concentrations of the products are in the numerator and that of the acid in the denominator. The water concentration is included in the constant.
96951.m: The acid dissociation constant is the law of mass action for the protolysis of an acid.

96952.q: Why does the concentration of water not appear in the expression for the acid dissociation constant?
a: It is practically constant in dilute solutions
Water does not take part in the reaction
Water has a concentration of zero
96952.e: In dilute solutions, the water concentration of about 55.5 mol/L hardly changes. So it is combined with the equilibrium constant to give Ka.
96952.m: The almost constant water concentration is already included in Ka.

96953.q: What does the acid dissociation constant of a particular acid in water depend on?
a: On the volume of the solution
96953.e: Like every equilibrium constant, Ka depends only on temperature for a given solvent. If you change the concentration, the equilibrium shifts, but Ka stays the same.
96953.m: Equilibrium constants only change with temperature.

96954.q: What is the equilibrium constant for the reaction of a weak base with water (B + H₂O ⇌ HB⁺ + OH⁻) called?
96954.e: For the protolysis of a base with water, the law of mass action is set up in the same way as for the acid constant. The constant obtained is called the base dissociation constant Kb; the larger it is, the stronger the base.
96954.m: The strength of a base is described by its base dissociation constant.

96955.q: What happens to the degree of protolysis of a weak acid if its solution is strongly diluted?
96955.e: According to Ostwald's dilution law, the equilibrium shifts towards the ions on dilution. A larger share of the acid molecules then gives off its proton.
96955.m: Diluted weak acids are protolysed to a greater percentage.

96956.q: A weak acid with a Ka of 10⁻⁵ mol/L is present at a concentration of 0.1 mol/L. Roughly what is the pH of the solution?
96956.e: For weak acids, c(H₃O⁺) is approximately the square root of Ka · c(HA), so the square root of 10⁻⁶, which gives 10⁻³ mol/L. The pH is therefore 3.
96956.m: For weak acids, you calculate with the square root of Ka times the concentration.

96957.q: Which of the following acids has the smallest Ka value?
96957.e: Hydrocyanic acid is a very weak acid with a Ka of about 6 · 10⁻¹⁰ mol/L. Hydrofluoric acid, formic acid and acetic acid have much larger acid constants.
96957.m: Hydrocyanic acid is a very weak acid.

96958.q: Acid A has a Ka of 10⁻³ mol/L and acid B a Ka of 10⁻⁶ mol/L. Which statement is correct?
a: Acid A is the stronger acid
Acid B is the stronger acid
96958.e: A larger Ka means that the protolysis equilibrium lies more on the side of the ions. Acid A has a Ka 1,000 times larger and is therefore stronger.
96958.m: The larger Ka is, the stronger the acid.

96959.q: How is the pKa value defined?
a: As the negative base-10 logarithm of Ka
As the natural logarithm of Ka
As the square root of Ka
96959.e: pKa equals −lg(Ka). This turns the very small values of Ka into handy numbers.
96959.m: The pKa is the negative base-10 logarithm of the acid constant.

96960.q: What does a small pKa value mean for the strength of an acid?
96960.e: Because of the negative sign in the logarithm, a small pKa belongs to a large Ka. So the acid readily gives off its proton.
96960.m: The smaller the pKa, the stronger the acid.

96961.q: Which pKa value best fits acetic acid, a typical weak acid?
96961.e: Weak acids have pKa values between about 4 and 10. At about 4.8, acetic acid is in the lower part of this range; strong acids such as hydrochloric acid have negative pKa values.
96961.m: With a pKa of just under 5, acetic acid is a weak acid.

96962.q: The ammonium ion has a pKa of 9.25. What is the pKb of ammonia at 25 °C?
96962.e: For a conjugate acid-base pair at 25 °C, pKa + pKb equals 14. So pKb equals 14 − 9.25, which is 4.75.
96962.m: At 25 °C, the pKa and pKb of a pair add up to 14.

96963.q: Why is the second pKa of phosphoric acid (7.21) much larger than the first (2.16)?
a: The proton has to be given off by a negatively charged ion
The second proton is lighter than the first
A gas forms in the second step
96963.e: After the first protolysis, H₂PO₄⁻ is present. Removing a proton from an ion that is already negatively charged is harder, because the attraction between the anion and the proton is greater.
96963.m: Polyprotic acids give off each further proton less easily.

96964.q: Acid X has a pKa of 3 and acid Y a pKa of 5. By what factor is the Ka of X larger?
96964.e: The pKa is a logarithmic quantity. A difference of 2 pKa units corresponds to a factor of 10 to the power of 2, so 100.
96964.m: Each pKa unit corresponds to a factor of ten in Ka.

96965.q: Why is hydrofluoric acid (HF) only a weak acid, despite the high electronegativity of fluorine?
a: The H-F bond is very strong
96965.e: The bond between hydrogen and the small fluorine atom is very strong and is hard to split in water. That is why HF has a pKa of about 3.2.
96965.m: The strength of the bond to hydrogen also counts for acid strength.

96966.q: Why is phenol (pKa about 10) a much stronger acid than ethanol (pKa about 16)?
a: The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance
96966.e: In the phenoxide ion, the negative charge can spread over the benzene ring. This resonance stabilisation is missing in the ethoxide ion.
96966.m: A stabilised base makes the corresponding acid stronger.

96967.q: Why is formic acid (HCOOH) slightly stronger than acetic acid (CH₃COOH)?
a: The methyl group pushes electrons and destabilises the acetate
Formic acid has more oxygen atoms
96967.e: The methyl group of acetic acid has a +I effect and increases the electron density at the carboxylate group. This makes the acetate ion less stable than the formate ion.

a: A mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base
A mixture of a strong acid and a strong base
A solution with no dissolved ions
96968.e: A buffer solution contains a weak acid and its conjugate base in similar amounts. As a result, the pH changes only a little when small amounts of acid or alkali are added.
96968.m: A buffer keeps the pH largely constant.

96969.q: Which mixture acts as a buffer?
a: Sodium hydroxide solution and table salt
96969.e: Acetic acid is a weak acid and acetate is its conjugate base. In the other mixtures, a strong acid or base is combined with a neutral salt.
96969.m: A buffer needs a weak conjugate acid-base pair.

96970.q: What happens if you add a little hydrochloric acid to an acetate buffer?
a: Acetate ions take up the protons and form acetic acid
The acetic acid gives off more protons
96970.e: The added oxonium ions react with acetate ions to form acetic acid and water. In this way they are mopped up and the pH falls only slightly.
96970.m: The base of the buffer mops up added acid.

96971.q: With what composition is the buffer capacity of a buffer greatest?
a: With equal amounts of acid and base
When only the acid is present
When only the base is present
With ten times more acid than base
96971.e: If acid and base are present in equal amounts, the buffer can mop up added acid and alkali equally well. The more uneven the ratio, the sooner one component is used up.
96971.m: A balanced ratio gives the greatest buffer capacity.

96972.q: In which pH range does a phosphate buffer of H₂PO₄⁻ and HPO₄²⁻ (pKa 7.21) buffer effectively?
96972.e: As a rule of thumb, a system buffers well in the range pKa plus or minus 1. For the phosphate buffer, that gives roughly pH 6.2 to 8.2.
96972.m: A buffer works about one pH unit either side of its pKa.

96973.q: How do you increase the buffer capacity without changing the pH of the buffer?
a: Make both components more concentrated in the same ratio
96973.e: The buffer capacity depends on the amount of buffer particles. If the ratio of base to acid stays the same, the pH stays the same too.
96973.m: More buffer particles mean more buffer capacity.

96974.q: What happens to the pH of a buffer if you dilute it moderately with water?
96974.e: When diluting, both concentrations change in the same ratio. Because the pH depends on the ratio, it stays almost unchanged; only the buffer capacity falls.
96974.m: Diluting hardly changes the pH of a buffer.

96975.q: Which buffer system is especially important inside cells?
96975.e: Phosphates are present in high concentrations in cells. So the pair H₂PO₄⁻ and HPO₄²⁻, together with proteins, buffers the pH inside cells.
96975.m: In cells, mainly phosphates and proteins act as buffers.

96976.q: What is typical of the titration curve of a strong acid with a strong base?
a: A steep jump in pH around pH 7
A gentle rise without a jump
96976.e: With strong acids and bases, the pH stays almost constant for a long time and then jumps by several units close to complete neutralisation. The jump is symmetrical around pH 7.
96976.m: A strong acid and a strong base give a large pH jump at pH 7.

96977.q: How does the pH jump of a weak acid differ from that of a strong acid of the same concentration?
a: It is smaller and starts at a higher pH
It is larger and starts at pH 0
96977.e: The weak acid is only slightly protolysed at first and forms a buffer during the titration. So the jump only starts at a higher pH and covers fewer pH units.
96977.m: Weak acids show a smaller pH jump than strong ones.

96978.q: Why is the titration curve of a weak acid with sodium hydroxide solution relatively flat before the jump?
a: A buffer forms from the acid and its salt
The sodium hydroxide does not react
96978.e: The added alkali produces the conjugate base of the weak acid. Together, the acid and base form a buffer system that dampens the rise in pH.
96978.m: In the flat part of the curve, the solution acts as a buffer.

96979.q: How can you recognise a polyprotic acid such as phosphoric acid in a titration curve?
a: By a straight line with no bend
96979.e: Each protolysis step is neutralised in turn. If the pKa values are different enough, the curve therefore shows several jumps.
96979.m: Polyprotic acids show several steps in the titration curve.

96980.q: Which indicator is suitable for titrating acetic acid with sodium hydroxide solution?
96980.e: Phenolphthalein changes colour between about pH 8.2 and 10, so it fits the jump in the slightly basic range. Methyl orange and methyl red change in the acidic range.
96980.m: The indicator's colour change range must lie within the pH jump.

96981.q: What is a titration called in which the electrical conductivity is measured instead of the pH?
96981.e: In conductometry, the conductivity of the solution is followed. Because H₃O⁺ and OH⁻ conduct especially well, the curve shows a kink at the neutralisation point.
96981.m: In conductometry, the conductivity is measured.

96982.q: With which measuring device is an acid-base titration curve usually recorded?
a: With a pH meter with a glass electrode
96982.e: A glass electrode measures the concentration of oxonium ions as an electrical voltage. The pH meter converts this into pH values, which are plotted against the volume added.
96982.m: A titration curve shows the pH against the volume of standard solution added.

96983.q: At what pH does the titration curve of hydrochloric acid with c equal to 0.1 mol/L start?
96983.e: Hydrochloric acid is completely protolysed, so c(H₃O⁺) equals 0.1 mol/L. The pH is −lg(0.1), so 1.
96983.m: For strong acids, c(H₃O⁺) equals the acid concentration.

96984.q: How much sodium hydroxide solution (c equal to 0.2 mol/L) is needed to reach the equivalence point if 15 mL of hydrochloric acid (c equal to 0.1 mol/L) is in the flask?
96984.e: The sample contains 0.015 L · 0.1 mol/L, which is 0.0015 mol of HCl. This amount of NaOH is in 0.0015 mol / 0.2 mol/L, which is 0.0075 L, so 7.5 mL.
96984.m: With an alkali twice as concentrated, you need only half as much.

96985.q: Which substance is dissolved at the equivalence point of the titration of sodium hydroxide solution with hydrochloric acid?
96985.e: Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide react to form water and sodium chloride. At the equivalence point both have reacted completely, leaving a salt solution.
96985.m: Neutralising hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide gives a salt solution.

96986.q: In which range is the equivalence point when ammonia solution is titrated with hydrochloric acid?
96986.e: At the equivalence point there is an ammonium chloride solution. Ammonium ions are weak acids and give off protons to water.
96986.m: With weak bases, the equivalence point is in the acidic range.

96987.q: 20 mL of hydrochloric acid is titrated with sodium hydroxide solution (c equal to 0.1 mol/L), and the equivalence point is at 25 mL. What is the concentration of the hydrochloric acid?
96987.e: Amount of NaOH used: 0.025 L · 0.1 mol/L equals 0.0025 mol, and the same amount of HCl. So c(HCl) equals 0.0025 mol / 0.020 L, which is 0.125 mol/L.
96987.m: At the equivalence point for monoprotic acids, c · V of the acid equals c · V of the base.

96989.q: What is the point in a titration at which the indicator changes colour called?
96989.e: The end point is shown by the indicator's colour change. With a well-chosen indicator, it is very close to the equivalence point.
96989.m: The colour change shows the end point of a titration.

96990.q: What amount of sodium hydroxide is needed to neutralise 0.5 mol of phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) to the third equivalence point?
96990.e: Phosphoric acid is triprotic, so each molecule reacts with three hydroxide ions to form phosphate. You therefore need 3 · 0.5 mol, so 1.5 mol of NaOH.
96990.m: With polyprotic acids, you count one hydroxide ion for each proton given off.

96991.q: How can the equivalence point be found graphically from a measured titration curve?
a: As the point of inflection in the steepest part of the pH jump
As the lowest point of the curve
As the point where it crosses the pH axis
96991.e: At the equivalence point, the pH changes most for each millilitre added. Mathematically that is the point of inflection of the curve, often found with the tangent method.
96991.m: The equivalence point is at the point of inflection of the titration curve.

a: A particle that can react as an acid and as a base
A particle that only takes up protons
96992.e: Depending on its reaction partner, an ampholyte can give off or take up protons. Water is the best-known example.
96992.m: An ampholyte can be both an acid and a base.

96993.e: Dihydrogen phosphate can give off a proton (to HPO₄²⁻) or take one up (to H₃PO₄). Phosphate and chloride can only take up protons, and ammonium can only give them off.
96993.m: Particles with a proton to give and a lone pair can be ampholytes.

96994.q: In what form are amino acids mainly found in neutral aqueous solution?
96994.e: The carboxyl group gives off a proton and the amino group takes one up. So the molecule carries a positive and a negative charge at the same time.
96994.m: Amino acids are ampholytes and form zwitterions.

96995.q: What is the pH at which an amino acid is electrically neutral overall called?
96995.e: At the isoelectric point, the amino acid is mainly present as a zwitterion and does not move in an electric field. It is different for each amino acid.
96995.m: At the isoelectric point, an amino acid has no net charge.

96996.q: Which metal hydroxide dissolves both in hydrochloric acid and in excess sodium hydroxide solution?
96996.e: Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric: with acids it forms aluminium salts, with alkalis soluble hydroxoaluminates. The other hydroxides only react as bases.
96996.m: Aluminium hydroxide is an amphoteric hydroxide.

96997.q: Which ion forms when zinc hydroxide dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution?
96997.e: Zinc hydroxide reacts with hydroxide ions to form the tetrahydroxozincate ion [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻. In acids, on the other hand, it forms Zn²⁺ ions.
96997.m: Zinc hydroxide dissolves in acids and in alkalis.

96998.q: What role does water play in the reaction with ammonia (NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻)?
a: It acts as a reducing agent
96998.e: Water gives a proton to ammonia, leaving a hydroxide ion behind. So in this reaction water is the proton donor.
96998.m: Towards ammonia, water behaves as an acid.

96999.q: What does the Greek word from which the term “amphoteric” is derived mean?
96999.e: In Greek, “amphoteros” means “both” or “each of two”. An amphoteric substance can take on both roles.
96999.m: Amphoteric substances can play both roles.

97000.q: Which equation describes the autoprotolysis of water?
97000.e: In autoprotolysis, one water molecule transfers a proton to another. This produces an oxonium ion and a hydroxide ion.
97000.m: In autoprotolysis, water reacts with itself.

97001.q: What is the value of the ionic product of water Kw at 25 °C?
97001.e: The ionic product is c(H₃O⁺) · c(OH⁻). At 25 °C it is 10⁻¹⁴ mol²/L².
97001.m: At 25 °C, the ionic product of water is 10 to the power of minus 14.

97002.q: What is the concentration of hydroxide ions in a solution with pH 4 at 25 °C?
97002.e: At pH 4, c(H₃O⁺) equals 10⁻⁴ mol/L. From the ionic product, c(OH⁻) equals 10⁻¹⁴ / 10⁻⁴, so 10⁻¹⁰ mol/L.
97002.m: Even acidic solutions always contain some hydroxide ions.

97003.q: A solution has a pOH of 3 at 25 °C. What is its pH?
97003.e: From autoprotolysis it follows that at 25 °C, pH + pOH equals 14. So pH equals 14 − 3, which gives 11.
97003.m: At 25 °C, pH and pOH add up to 14.

97004.q: Why is the pH of pure water at 60 °C less than 7, even though the water stays neutral?
a: Autoprotolysis is endothermic, so Kw becomes larger
Water takes up salt when heated
Only oxonium ions form when it is heated
97004.e: Because autoprotolysis takes in heat, the equilibrium shifts towards the ions on heating. More H₃O⁺ forms and the same number of OH⁻, so the water stays neutral.
97004.m: Neutral means equal numbers of oxonium and hydroxide ions, not always pH 7.

97005.q: Which ions form in the autoprotolysis of liquid ammonia?
97005.e: Liquid ammonia also undergoes protolysis to a very small extent: one molecule gives a proton to another. This produces ammonium and amide ions.
97005.m: Autoprotolysis also happens in solvents other than water.

97006.q: Why does ultrapure water conduct electricity only extremely weakly?
a: Only a tiny share of the molecules is protolysed
Water contains no ions at all
97006.e: Because of autoprotolysis, only very few ions are present. Only dissolved salts, acids or bases provide enough charge carriers for good conductivity.
97006.m: Pure water contains only very few ions.

97007.q: In pure water at 25 °C, roughly how many water molecules are there for each oxonium ion?
97007.e: Water has a concentration of about 55.5 mol/L, oxonium ions 10⁻⁷ mol/L. The ratio 55.5 / 10⁻⁷ gives about 5.55 · 10⁸.
97007.m: Autoprotolysis affects only a tiny fraction of the water molecules.

97008.q: How is an acid defined according to Lewis?
97008.e: According to Lewis, an acid takes up a lone pair from a base. This forms a covalent bond between the two.
97008.m: A Lewis acid takes up an electron pair.

97009.q: Which substance is a typical Lewis acid?
97009.e: Boron trifluoride can take up another particle's electron pair. Ammonia, fluoride and methanol have lone pairs and act as Lewis bases.
97009.m: Boron trifluoride is a classic example of a Lewis acid.

97010.q: Why does boron trifluoride (BF₃) act as a Lewis acid?
a: The boron atom has only an electron sextet
BF₃ has a lone pair on the boron
97010.e: In BF₃, boron forms only three bonds and so has six instead of eight valence electrons. The empty orbital can take up an electron pair to reach the octet.
97010.m: A lack of electrons makes a particle a Lewis acid.

97011.q: Which particle is a Lewis base?
97011.e: Ammonia has a lone pair on the nitrogen that it can donate. The other three particles are short of electrons and act as Lewis acids.
97011.m: A Lewis base has a lone pair that it can donate.

97012.q: What role does the Cu²⁺ ion play in the formation of the tetraamminecopper(II) complex?
a: It acts as a Lewis acid
It acts as a Lewis base
It acts as a Brønsted base
It acts as a reducing agent
97012.e: The four ammonia molecules each provide a lone pair. The copper ion takes up these electron pairs and forms coordinate bonds.
97012.m: Central ions in complexes are Lewis acids.

97013.q: Which chemist defined acids as electron pair acceptors in 1923?
97013.e: In 1923, the American chemist Gilbert Newton Lewis extended the idea of an acid to electron pairs. This means reactions without protons can also be described as acid-base reactions.
97013.m: Lewis explained acids and bases in terms of electron pairs.

97014.q: Which statement about the acid-base theories is correct?
a: Every Brønsted base is also a Lewis base
Lewis bases have no lone pairs
Brønsted acids take up electron pairs
97014.e: To bind a proton, a base needs a lone pair. So every Brønsted base also meets the definition of a Lewis base.
97014.m: The Lewis theory is broader than the Brønsted theory.

97015.q: What is the product formed when BF₃ reacts with NH₃ called?
97015.e: Ammonia binds to the boron atom with its lone pair. This forms the adduct H₃N-BF₃ with a coordinate bond.
97015.m: A Lewis acid and a Lewis base together form an adduct.

97016.q: Why is the proton H⁺ itself also regarded as a Lewis acid?
a: It can take a lone pair into its empty orbital
97016.e: A proton has no electrons and an empty 1s orbital. When it binds to a base, it takes up the base's electron pair.
97016.m: The proton is an electron pair acceptor.

97017.q: Which of these acids is a strong acid?
97017.e: Nitric acid (HNO₃) is practically completely protolysed in water. Acetic acid, carbonic acid and hydrocyanic acid are weak acids.
97017.m: Nitric acid is one of the strong mineral acids.

97018.q: What is typical of a strong acid in dilute aqueous solution?
97018.e: With a strong acid, the protolysis equilibrium lies almost completely on the side of the ions. Nearly all the acid molecules have given their proton to water.
97018.m: Strong acids give off their protons almost completely in water.

97019.q: What is the pH of hydrochloric acid with a concentration of 0.01 mol/L?
97019.e: Hydrochloric acid is completely protolysed, so c(H₃O⁺) equals 0.01 mol/L or 10⁻² mol/L. The pH is the negative exponent, so 2.
97019.m: For strong acids, the pH comes directly from the concentration.

97020.q: Acetic acid (Ka about 1.75 · 10⁻⁵ mol/L) is present at a concentration of 0.1 mol/L. Roughly what is the pH of the solution?
97020.e: For weak acids, c(H₃O⁺) equals the square root of Ka · c, so the square root of 1.75 · 10⁻⁶, which is about 1.3 · 10⁻³ mol/L. The pH is therefore about 2.9.
97020.m: At the same concentration, a weak acid has a higher pH than a strong one.

97021.q: Why do hydrochloric acid and perchloric acid appear equally strong in water?
a: Both are completely protolysed to oxonium ions
Both have the same molecular mass
Both contain chlorine in the acid residue
97021.e: In water, H₃O⁺ is the strongest acid that can exist. All stronger acids are completely converted to H₃O⁺; this is called the levelling effect of water.
97021.m: Water evens out the strength of very strong acids.

97022.q: Hydrochloric acid with pH 2 is diluted with water in the ratio 1 to 100. What is its pH afterwards?
97022.e: Diluting by a factor of 100 lowers c(H₃O⁺) from 10⁻² to 10⁻⁴ mol/L. So the pH rises by 2 units to 4.
97022.m: Diluting a strong acid tenfold raises the pH by one.

97023.q: What does the strength of an acid tell you?
a: How completely it gives off protons in water
How much acid is dissolved per litre
How corrosive it is on the skin
97023.e: Acid strength describes the position of the protolysis equilibrium. So a dilute strong acid can be less acidic than a concentrated weak acid.
97023.m: The strength and the concentration of an acid are different things.

97024.q: Which hydrohalic acid is the strongest in water?
97024.e: From HF to HI the atoms get larger and the bond to hydrogen gets weaker. So HI gives off its proton most easily.
97024.m: The acid strength of the hydrogen halides increases from top to bottom.

97025.q: Which statement about sulphuric acid in water is correct?
a: The first step is strong, the second much weaker
It only gives off a single proton
The second step is stronger than the first
97025.e: H₂SO₄ gives off its first proton completely. With a pKa of about 1.9, the hydrogen sulphate ion HSO₄⁻ is only a moderately strong acid.
97025.m: In its first step, sulphuric acid is a strong acid.

97026.q: In which pH range is the normal value of human arterial blood?
97026.e: Blood pH is kept within a very narrow range between 7.35 and 7.45. Values below this are called acidosis, values above it alkalosis.
97026.m: Blood is slightly basic and tightly buffered.

97027.q: Which enzyme speeds up the reaction of CO₂ with water to form carbonic acid in the body?
97027.e: Carbonic anhydrase, found for example in red blood cells, speeds up reaching equilibrium enormously. Without it, the reaction would be far too slow for the body.
97027.m: Carbonic anhydrase makes the bicarbonate buffer fast.

97028.q: Which organ regulates the hydrogen carbonate concentration in the blood in the long term?
97028.e: The kidneys can recover or excrete hydrogen carbonate and give off protons. This regulation works more slowly than breathing, but it lasts.
97028.m: The kidney controls the hydrogen carbonate level of the blood in the long term.

97029.q: Which disturbance of the acid-base balance is caused by strong hyperventilation?
97029.e: Breathing too fast breathes out a lot of CO₂. As a result the carbonic acid concentration falls and the pH of the blood rises.
97029.m: Breathing out too much CO₂ makes the blood more basic.

97030.q: At pH 7.4, roughly what is the ratio of hydrogen carbonate to dissolved CO₂ in the blood (pKa equal to 6.1)?
97030.e: From 7.4 equals 6.1 + lg(ratio), it follows that lg(ratio) equals 1.3. Ten to the power of 1.3 gives about 20.
97030.m: In the blood, hydrogen carbonate clearly outweighs dissolved CO₂.

97031.q: Why does the carbonic acid system buffer the blood well, even though its pKa (6.1) is far from 7.4?
a: It is an open system; CO₂ is breathed out through the lungs
97031.e: Extra acid produces CO₂, which can be released through the lungs straight away. Because the CO₂ concentration is kept constant in this way, the buffer is much more effective than in a closed vessel.
97031.m: Breathing makes the carbonic acid buffer an open system.

97032.q: How does the body compensate for metabolic acidosis in the short term, for example in diabetic ketoacidosis?
97032.e: The stronger breathing, known as Kussmaul breathing, releases more CO₂. This lowers the carbonic acid concentration and the pH rises again.
97032.m: The lungs can quickly partly correct an over-acidic blood.

97033.q: What is the result of the oceans taking up extra CO₂ from the air?
a: More oxygen forms in the water
97033.e: Dissolved CO₂ forms carbonic acid, which releases protons. This ocean acidification reduces the amount of carbonate ions that shellfish and corals need for their limestone shells.
97033.m: More CO₂ in the air leads to the acidification of the seas.

97034.e: The equation links the pH of a buffer with the pKa and the ratio of base to acid. More base in the ratio raises the pH.
97034.m: The pH of a buffer depends on the pKa and the ratio of base to acid.

97035.q: An acetate buffer (pKa 4.76) contains ten times more acetate than acetic acid. What is its pH?
97035.e: According to Henderson-Hasselbalch, pH equals 4.76 + lg(10). Because lg(10) equals 1, this gives 5.76.
97035.m: A tenfold excess of base raises the pH one unit above the pKa.

97036.q: One litre of acetate buffer (pKa 4.76) contains 0.2 mol each of acetic acid and acetate. Roughly what pH results after adding 0.05 mol of HCl?
97036.e: The hydrochloric acid converts 0.05 mol of acetate into acetic acid: 0.15 mol of acetate and 0.25 mol of acetic acid. pH equals 4.76 + lg(0.15 / 0.25), which is 4.76 − 0.22, so about 4.54.
97036.m: After adding acid, you calculate with the new amounts of acid and base.

97037.q: A phosphate buffer (pKa 7.21) is to have pH 7.51. In what ratio must HPO₄²⁻ and H₂PO₄⁻ be present?
97037.e: lg(ratio) equals 7.51 − 7.21, so 0.30. Ten to the power of 0.30 gives about 2.
97037.m: With the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation you can set up buffers precisely.

97038.q: What is the pH of a buffer that contains equal amounts of a weak acid and its conjugate base?
97038.e: According to Henderson-Hasselbalch, pH equals pKa + lg(1). Because lg(1) equals 0, the pH is exactly the pKa.
97038.m: With equal amounts of acid and base, the pH equals the pKa.

97039.q: When does the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation give inaccurate results?
a: With very dilute buffers or a very uneven ratio
97039.e: The equation assumes that the concentrations of acid and base hardly change through protolysis. With very small concentrations or extreme ratios, this is no longer true.
97039.m: The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is an approximation.

97040.q: How is the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation derived?
a: By taking the logarithm of the expression for the acid constant
97040.e: You solve the Ka expression for c(H₃O⁺) and take the negative base-10 logarithm. This gives pH, pKa and the logarithm of the concentration ratio.
97040.m: The buffer equation is the law of mass action in logarithmic form.

97041.q: An ammonia buffer (pKa of NH₄⁺ equal to 9.25) contains ten times more NH₄⁺ than NH₃. What is its pH?
97041.e: The base is NH₃ and the acid NH₄⁺. pH equals 9.25 + lg(1/10), which is 9.25 − 1, so 8.25.
97041.m: An excess of acid lowers the pH below the pKa.

97241.q: What is wheat mainly made into?
97241.e: The wheat grains are ground into fine flour. Bread and cakes are baked from it.
97241.m: Bread is baked from wheat flour.

97242.q: What is the top part of the wheat stalk, where the grains sit, called?
97242.e: In wheat, the grains sit tightly packed in the ear. The ear grows at the top of the stalk.
97242.m: Wheat grains sit in the ear.

97243.q: Which group of plants does wheat belong to?
97243.e: Wheat is a cereal, like barley, rye and oats. Cereals are grasses with edible grains.

97244.q: Which kind of wheat is used to make spaghetti and other pasta?
97244.e: Pasta is usually made from durum wheat. It is ground into semolina and makes firm spaghetti.
97244.m: Spaghetti is usually made from durum wheat.

97245.q: The flour of which cereal is used to bake the Sunday Zopf, the plaited bread?
97245.e: Zopf is baked from wheat flour, milk, butter and yeast. Wheat flour makes the dough nice and fine and light.
97245.m: Zopf is baked from wheat flour.

97246.q: When does the farmer sow most wheat?
97246.e: Most wheat is winter wheat. It is sown in autumn, grows a little and spends the winter in the field.
97246.m: Winter wheat is sown in autumn.

97247.q: Where are wheat grains ground into flour?
97247.e: At the mill, rollers crush the grains into fine flour. In the past, water or wind turned the mill wheels.
97247.m: Grain is ground into flour at the mill.

97248.q: How can you easily recognise barley in the field?
97248.e: Barley has long, fine bristles on its ears. They are called awns and look like a beard.
97248.m: You can recognise barley by its long awns.

97249.q: Which canton does the well-known barley soup come from?
97249.e: Grisons barley soup is a well-known dish from the Grisons. It contains barley grains, vegetables and often bacon or meat.
97249.m: Barley soup is a well-known dish from the Grisons.

97250.q: What is a lot of barley used for in Switzerland?
97250.e: A large part of the barley is fed to animals such as pigs and cattle. Barley is a good feed grain.
97250.m: Barley is an important animal feed.

97251.q: Which cereal is usually harvested first in summer?
97251.e: Winter barley ripens early. It is often harvested at the end of June or in July, before the wheat.
97251.m: Barley is usually harvested before wheat.

97252.q: What do you get when barley grains sprout and are then dried?
97252.e: Sprouted and dried barley is called malt. Malt is used, for example, for malted drinks.
97252.m: Malt is made from sprouted barley.

97253.q: How long have people been growing barley?
97253.e: Barley is one of the oldest crops. People have been growing it for about 10,000 years.
97253.m: Barley is one of the oldest crops.

97254.q: What are hulled and polished barley grains for soup called?
97254.e: Pearl barley is made of round, hulled barley grains. It is cooked in soups.
97254.m: Pearl barley goes into barley soup.

97255.q: What is the thick part of the maize plant where the kernels sit called?
97255.e: In maize, the kernels sit in rows on the cob. The cob is wrapped in green leaves.
97255.m: Maize kernels sit on the cob.

97256.q: What colour are the kernels of feed maize usually?
97256.e: Most maize kernels are yellow. But there are also varieties with white, red or blue kernels.

97257.q: What pops in the pan when you heat special maize kernels?
97257.e: Popcorn maize contains a little water. When heated, it turns into steam and the kernel bursts open into popcorn.
97257.m: Popcorn maize turns into popcorn when heated.

97258.q: Which dish from Ticino is made from maize meal?
97258.e: Polenta is a porridge made from maize meal. In Ticino it is often eaten with meat, mushrooms or cheese.
97258.m: Polenta is made from maize meal.

97259.q: Which continent does maize originally come from?
97259.e: Maize was grown in Mexico thousands of years ago. Sailors later brought it to Europe.

97260.q: How tall can a maize plant grow in summer?
a: As tall as a blade of grass
As tall as a church tower
97260.e: Maize grows quickly and often reaches more than 2 metres. That is why you cannot see over a maize field.
97260.m: Maize grows taller than a person.

a: A maze of paths in a maize field
A house made of maize straw
97261.e: For a maize maze, paths are cut into the tall maize field. You have to find your way to the exit.
97261.m: In a maize maze you look for the way to the exit.

97262.q: What colour are the flowers of oilseed rape?
97262.e: When rape is in flower, the fields glow yellow. You can see them from far away.

97263.q: What is made from the seeds of oilseed rape?
97263.e: The small rapeseeds contain a lot of fat. They are pressed to get rapeseed oil.

97264.q: In which season does oilseed rape flower?
97264.e: Rape usually flowers in April and May. It is then harvested in summer.

97265.q: Which animals like to collect nectar from rape flowers?
97265.e: Rape flowers have lots of nectar and pollen. Bees make rapeseed honey from them.
97265.m: Bees love to fly to rape flowers.

97266.e: Rapeseeds are tiny, round, blackish-brown balls. They are about the size of a pinhead.
97266.m: Rapeseeds are small, round and dark.

97267.q: What do rapeseeds grow in after flowering?
97267.e: After flowering, rape forms long, thin pods. The seeds ripen inside them until summer.

97268.q: What is rapeseed oil used for in the kitchen?
97268.e: Rapeseed oil can be used for salad dressings and for frying. It is one of the most important cooking oils in Switzerland.
97268.m: Rapeseed oil is a cooking oil for salad and frying.

97269.q: Roughly how tall is an oilseed rape plant when it is in flower?
97269.e: Flowering rape grows about one to one and a half metres tall. It reaches over the heads of small children.
97269.m: Rape grows about a metre tall.

97270.q: What is made from sugar beet?
97270.e: Sugar beet contains a lot of sugar. In the factory it is extracted and dried.
97270.m: Sugar is made from sugar beet.

97271.q: Where does the part of the sugar beet that holds the sugar grow?
97271.e: The thick beet grows under the ground. Only the green leaves stick out at the top.
97271.m: Sugar beet grows in the ground.

97272.q: What colour is a sugar beet inside?
97272.e: Sugar beet is white inside. Red beetroot is a different kind of beet.

97273.q: In which season is sugar beet harvested?
97273.e: Sugar beet is harvested from about September to November. Then it is taken to the sugar factory.
97273.m: Sugar beet is harvested in autumn.

97274.q: In which two Swiss towns are there sugar factories?
97274.e: Swiss sugar beet is processed in Aarberg in the canton of Bern and in Frauenfeld in Thurgau.
97274.m: Swiss sugar comes from Aarberg and Frauenfeld.

97275.q: What often lies in big heaps at the edge of fields in autumn?
97275.e: After the harvest, sugar beet is stored at the edge of the field. Lorries or trains then take it to the factory.
97275.m: In autumn, sugar beet lies in heaps at the edge of fields.

97276.q: What colour are the leaves of sugar beet in the field?
97276.e: The leaves of the sugar beet are green. With their help the plant makes sugar from sunlight.

97277.q: Roughly how heavy is a large sugar beet?
97277.e: A sugar beet usually weighs about one kilogram. Some get even heavier.
97277.m: A sugar beet weighs about one kilogram.

97278.q: What kind of bread is made from rye?
97278.e: Rye flour is darker than wheat flour. It is used to bake dark, hearty bread.
97278.m: Dark bread is baked from rye.

97279.q: Which canton is a famous dark rye bread from?
97279.e: Valais rye bread is known all over Switzerland. It has to be baked in Valais.
97279.m: Valais rye bread comes from Valais.

97280.q: What can rye cope with especially well?
97280.e: Rye copes well with cold and also grows on poor soil. That is why it used to be grown in mountain valleys such as in Valais.

97281.q: When is rye harvested in the field?
97281.e: In summer the rye is ripe and dry. Then the farmers drive onto the field with the combine harvester.

97282.q: What are rye stalks like compared with wheat?
97282.e: Rye has long stalks and often grows taller than wheat. Its straw is therefore especially long.

97283.q: What colour is a field of ripe rye?
97283.e: When the rye is ripe, the stalks and ears are dry and yellowish brown. Then it can be harvested.

97284.q: Which crispy, flat bread is often made from rye?
97284.e: Crispbread comes from Scandinavia and is traditionally baked from rye flour. It is thin, dry and crispy.
97284.m: Crispbread is often made from rye.

97285.q: How does rye bread taste compared with white bread?
97285.e: Rye bread is often baked with sourdough. That is why it tastes strong and slightly sour.
97285.m: Rye bread tastes strong and slightly sour.

97286.q: What is removed from the oat grain in the mill before flakes are made?
97286.e: The oat grain sits inside a hard husk. In the mill it is removed, then flakes are made from the grain.
97286.m: The oat grain has a hard husk.

97287.e: To make oat flakes, the grains are pressed flat between rollers. That is why the flakes are thin and flat.
97287.m: Oat flakes are oat grains rolled flat.

97288.q: What do oats need especially a lot of to grow?
97288.e: Oats grow well where it is cool and rains often. In a long dry spell they quickly suffer.
97288.m: Oats need a lot of water.

97289.q: Roughly how many grains are there in an ear of wheat?
97289.e: An ear of wheat usually holds about 30 to 50 grains. A whole field carries millions of them.
97289.m: An ear of wheat holds a few dozen grains.

97290.q: How do oat grains hang on the plant?
97290.e: In oats, the grains hang loosely on many thin little branches. Wheat and barley, on the other hand, have a dense ear.
97290.m: Oats carry their grains on thin little branches.

97291.q: What warm breakfast is often made from oat flakes and milk?
97291.e: Oat flakes are cooked with milk or water. This makes a warm oat porridge.
97291.m: Porridge is cooked from oat flakes and milk.

97292.q: What do some people drink oat drink instead of?
97292.e: Oat drink is made from oats and water. It looks pale like milk, and some people drink it instead of cow's milk.
97292.m: Some people drink oat drink instead of milk.

97293.q: Which hot drink can be made from roasted barley?
97293.e: Roasted barley tastes similar to coffee. Barley coffee, however, has no caffeine.
97293.m: Barley coffee is made from roasted barley.

97294.q: What might a tractor pull on the field, for example?
97294.e: The tractor is strong and pulls equipment such as a plough or trailer. This lets the farmer work the field.
97294.m: A tractor pulls equipment such as the plough.

97295.q: What fuel do most tractors run on?
97295.e: Most tractors have a powerful diesel engine. But there are also the first tractors with electric motors.

97296.q: What is the shovel at the front of a tractor called, used to lift heavy things?
97296.e: With the front loader the farmer lifts bales or soil, for example. The shovel can also be swapped for a fork.
97296.m: With the front loader the tractor lifts heavy loads.

97297.q: Which wheels are especially big on many tractors?
97297.e: Many tractors have very big wheels at the back. They carry a lot of weight and give a lot of pulling power.
97297.m: Many tractors have big rear wheels.

97298.q: With which machine does the tractor spread seeds on the field?
97298.e: The seed drill puts the seeds into the soil in rows. The tractor pulls it across the field.
97298.m: Seeds are sown with the seed drill.

97299.q: From what age may you drive a small tractor in Switzerland with a category G licence?
97299.e: With a category G driving licence, young people aged 14 and over may drive agricultural vehicles up to 30 km/h. A test is required for this.
97299.m: In Switzerland you may drive a tractor with a licence from age 14.

97300.q: Which tool does the tractor pull to make the soil fine after ploughing?
97300.e: The harrow breaks up rough clods of earth. This makes the soil fine and ready for sowing.
97300.m: The harrow makes the soil fine.

97301.q: Where does the driver sit on a modern tractor?
97301.e: Modern tractors have a cab with windows. It protects the driver from rain, dust and noise.
97301.m: The driver sits in the tractor's cab.

97302.q: In which month is a lot of grain harvested in Switzerland?
97302.e: The grain harvest takes place mainly in July and August. Then the grains are ripe and dry.

97303.q: What weather does the farmer need for the grain harvest?
97303.e: Wet grain is hard to harvest and can go mouldy. That is why the farmer waits for dry days.
97303.m: Grain is harvested in dry weather.

97304.q: What did people use in the past to cut grain by hand?
97304.e: In the past, farmers cut the grain with a scythe or a sickle. That was very hard work.
97304.m: In the past, grain was cut with a scythe.

97305.q: Where do grains go after the harvest so that they stay dry?
97305.e: The grains are stored in big containers called silos. There they stay dry and clean.
97305.m: Grain is stored in a silo.

97306.q: How does a farmer often check whether the grain is ripe?
97306.e: A ripe grain is hard and dry and can barely be bitten through. If it is still soft, the farmer waits to harvest.
97306.m: Ripe grains are hard and dry.

97307.q: What was a bundle of cut grain stalks called in the past?
97307.e: In the past, the stalks were tied together into sheaves. The sheaves were stood up in the field to dry.
97307.m: A bundle of grain stalks is called a sheaf.

97308.q: What is left lying on the field once the grains have been harvested?
97308.e: The combine harvester only takes the grains. The dry stalks fall onto the field as straw.
97308.m: After the grain harvest, the straw is left lying.

97309.q: What are the short bits of stalk left standing in the field after the harvest called?
97309.e: After mowing, short, hard pieces of stalk stay standing in the ground. Such a field is called a stubble field.
97309.m: After the harvest, a stubble field is left.

97310.q: What does a combine harvester do?
97310.e: The combine harvester cuts the stalks and at once separates the grains from the straw. It does two jobs in one.
97310.m: The combine harvester cuts and threshes in one.

97311.q: Where does the combine harvester collect the harvested grains?
97311.e: The grains flow into a big tank on top of the combine harvester. When it is full, they are emptied into a trailer.
97311.m: The combine harvester collects the grains in the grain tank.

97312.q: What does the big rotating drum at the front of the combine harvester do?
a: It pushes the stalks towards the blade
97312.e: The drum is called a reel. It turns slowly and pushes the stalks against the blade. This cuts them off cleanly.
97312.m: The reel guides the stalks to the blade.

97313.q: Apart from grain, what else can a combine harvester harvest?
97313.e: With the right cutting unit, the combine harvester also threshes rapeseed or peas. Potatoes and beet need their own harvesting machines.
97313.m: The combine harvester also harvests rapeseed.

97314.q: How is the grain trailer filled when the combine harvester's tank is full?
97314.e: The combine harvester has a long pipe sticking out to the side. Through it, the grains flow into the trailer next to it.
97314.m: The combine harvester empties the grains through a long pipe.

97315.q: Where does the combine harvester cut the stalks?
a: Right at the top by the ears
Under the ground by the roots
It doesn't, it pulls them out
97315.e: The wide cutting unit at the front of the combine harvester has a long blade. It cuts the stalks just above the ground.
97315.m: The cutting unit cuts the stalks just above the ground.

97316.q: When do you see combine harvesters in the fields?
97316.e: Combine harvesters work mainly in summer when the grain is ripe. For grain maize also in autumn.
97316.m: You see combine harvesters mainly in summer.

97317.q: Why does a combine harvester drive slowly and carefully on the road?
a: Because it has only three wheels
97317.e: Combine harvesters are wide and heavy. On the road, the cutting unit is often taken off and towed behind on a trailer.
97317.m: A combine harvester is very wide on the road.

97318.e: Straw is the dry stalks of grain after the harvest. Dried grass, on the other hand, is called hay.

97319.q: What is straw used for in the barn?
a: As a soft bed for the animals
As the main food for cows
97319.e: Straw is spread out in the barn. It is soft and soaks up dung and urine.
97319.m: Straw is bedding for animals in the barn.

97320.q: Which machine turns loose straw into firm bales?
97320.e: The baler picks up the straw from the field and presses it tightly together. Then the bale is tied with twine or net.
97320.m: The baler makes bales out of straw.

97321.q: Which two shapes do straw bales usually have?
97321.e: There are round bales that look like big rolls and square, box-shaped bales. Both are made by balers.
97321.m: Straw bales are round or square.

97322.q: What colour is a straw bale?
97322.e: Straw is dry and pale yellow like ripe grain. Fresh grass, on the other hand, is green.

97323.q: What do people like to make from straws at Christmas time?
97323.e: Shiny straws are tied into stars. They are hung on the Christmas tree or in the window.
97323.m: You can make Christmas stars from straw.

97324.q: Why must straw bales be stored dry?
97324.e: Wet straw starts to rot and go mouldy. That is why bales are stored under a roof or wrapped in plastic.

97325.q: What are round bales often held together with?
97325.e: The baler wraps a net or twine around the bale. That way it doesn't fall apart when it is moved.
97325.m: A net holds round bales together.

97326.q: What else is a trained farmer called?
97326.e: Anyone who runs a farm and has trained for it is an agriculturalist. In Switzerland the apprenticeship lasts three years.
97326.m: A farmer is also called an agriculturalist.

97327.q: In which building on the farm are hay and straw stored?
97327.e: The barn is a big building for storage. There, hay, straw and equipment stay dry.
97327.m: Hay and straw are stored in the barn.

97328.q: Where can you buy eggs or potatoes directly on the farm?
97328.e: Many farms have a small farm shop. There they sell what grows on the farm.
97328.m: In the farm shop you buy directly from the farmer.

97329.q: What does the farmer put in the field to scare away birds?
97329.e: A scarecrow looks like a person. It is meant to stop birds from eating the seeds.
97329.m: A scarecrow scares birds away from the field.

97330.q: Why doesn't the farmer plant the same thing in the same field every year?
97330.e: The farmer changes the crops, for example wheat, then maize, then beet. This is called crop rotation, and it keeps the soil healthy.
97330.m: Crop rotation keeps the soil healthy.

97331.q: What does the farmer spread on the fields as natural fertiliser?
97331.e: Manure is a mixture of dung and straw from the barn. It gives nutrients back to the soil.

97332.q: What is a field where the farmer grows grain or beet called?
97332.e: An arable field is ploughed and sown. On a pasture, by contrast, grass grows for the animals.
97332.m: Grain and beet grow on arable fields.

97333.q: Where is manure kept on the farm before it goes onto the field?
97333.e: The manure from the barn is collected on a pile called the manure heap. Later the farmer takes it to the field.
97333.m: Manure is collected on the manure heap.

97334.q: Which machine does the farmer hitch to the tractor to spread manure on the field?
97334.e: The manure spreader is a trailer with turning rollers at the back. They throw the manure evenly over the field.
97334.m: Manure is spread on the field with the manure spreader.

97335.q: Which crispy breakfast flakes are made from maize?
97335.e: For cornflakes, maize is cooked, rolled flat and toasted. Here the word “corn” means maize.

97336.q: For which celebration do many Swiss farms invite people to a big breakfast?
97336.e: On the national holiday many farms hold the farmers' breakfast, the 1 August brunch. People eat plaited bread, cheese and butter from the farm.
97336.m: On 1 August many farms hold a brunch.

97337.q: What do cows get from sugar beet once the sugar has been extracted?
97337.e: After the sugar is extracted, small pieces of beet are left over. This pulp is good feed for cows.
97337.m: The leftovers of sugar beet are feed for cows.

97338.q: What is separating the grains from the stalks called?
97338.e: When threshing, the grains are beaten out of the ears. In the past this was done by hand with a flail.
97338.m: Threshing separates the grains from the straw.

97339.q: How do people often show joy on their face?
a: With drooping corners of the mouth
97339.e: When you are happy, the corners of your mouth go up. That makes a smile.
97339.m: Joy often shows as a smile.

97340.q: What feeling do most children have at a great birthday party?
97340.e: A lovely party with presents and friends makes you happy. That feeling is called joy.

97341.q: What do many children do when they are really, really happy?
97341.e: Great joy is full of energy. Many children jump, clap or shout out loud.
97341.m: Great joy gets the body moving.

97342.q: What often happens when you make someone happy?
97342.e: When you do something nice for others, you often feel good yourself. Joy can be passed on.
97342.m: Making others happy often makes you happy too.

97343.q: What do you call loud, bubbling joy in a group?
97343.e: When a goal is scored in a football stadium, lots of people cheer at the same time. Cheering is joy shown out loud.

97344.q: Which word describes a person who is happy?
97344.e: Cheerful means full of joy. The other words belong to other feelings.
97344.m: A cheerful person is full of joy.

97345.q: How do many people feel after exercise in the fresh air?
97345.e: When you move, the body makes substances that put you in a good mood. That is why you often feel better afterwards.
97345.m: Exercise in the fresh air lifts your mood.

97346.q: What is a jump for joy?
a: A jump because you are so happy
97346.e: When they get very good news, some people jump into the air. This is called a jump for joy.
97346.m: You jump for joy out of sheer happiness.

97347.q: What can you do to remember happy moments?
a: Write them down or draw them
97347.e: If you write down or draw happy experiences, you can look at them again later. Then the joy comes back.
97347.m: You can write down or draw happy moments.

97348.q: Which organ often beats faster when you are afraid?
97348.e: When you are afraid, the body gets ready to react quickly. The heart then pumps blood faster.
97348.m: When you are afraid, your heart beats faster.

a: It makes you full more quickly
97349.e: Fear makes us careful. For example, it stops us going too close to a cliff edge.

97350.q: What are many children afraid of at night?
97350.e: You can't see much in the dark. So many children imagine things that frighten them.
97350.m: Many children are afraid of the dark.

97351.q: What helps many children with fear of the dark?
97351.e: A dim light shows that everything in the room is fine. Many children sleep more calmly with one.
97351.m: A night light can ease fear of the dark.

97352.q: What does the body often do when you get a big fright?
97352.e: When you get a fright, your body flinches very quickly. It happens without thinking.
97352.m: When you get a fright, you flinch.

97353.q: What is a good thing to do if a fear has been bothering you for a long time?
97353.e: Talking about your fear often makes you feel lighter. Parents or teachers can help.
97353.m: You should talk to someone about your fears.

97354.q: Which animal often plays dead when in danger?
97354.e: The opossum lives in America. When in danger it falls over and lies stiff until the danger has passed.
97354.m: The opossum plays dead when in danger.

97355.q: What often helps when you are nervous or scared?
a: Holding your breath for a long time
97355.e: Calm, deep breathing calms the heart. That way you become calmer again.

97356.q: What do some people get on their skin when they are scared or cold?
97356.e: When you are scared or cold, the tiny hairs stand up. The skin then looks like a plucked goose.
97356.m: You can get goosebumps when you are scared.

97357.q: What helps when you are very angry?
97357.e: Counting slowly gives you time. The anger usually gets smaller.
97357.m: Counting to ten helps against anger.

97358.q: What do your eyebrows usually look like when you are angry?
97358.e: When you are angry, you pull your eyebrows down and together. This often makes a wrinkle above the nose.
97358.m: When you are angry, you draw your eyebrows together.

97359.q: What colour does your face sometimes go when you are angry?
97359.e: When you are angry, more blood flows into your face. That is why it often turns red.
97359.m: Your face can go red when you are angry.

97360.q: Germans have a saying for great anger: someone is “at ...”. Which number is missing?
97360.e: The German saying “to be at one hundred and eighty” means that someone is very worked up or angry.
97360.m: In the German saying, someone “at one hundred and eighty” is very angry.

97361.e: Everyone gets angry sometimes. The important thing is not to hurt anyone.

97362.q: What do you call a small child's violent outburst of anger?
97362.e: Small children are not yet good at controlling their anger. They scream or throw themselves on the floor.

97363.q: How do you show your anger without hurting anyone?
a: You tear up an exercise book
97363.e: If you say in words what is annoying you, you don't hurt anyone. That way you can also sort out the argument.
97363.m: You can show anger with words.

97364.q: Which word means almost the same as anger?
97364.e: Rage and anger mean almost the same. Both describe strong annoyance.
97364.m: Rage is another word for anger.

97365.q: What do you call someone who gets angry very quickly?
97365.e: A hothead gets angry quickly. Their head gets hot fast, so to speak.

97366.q: What do many people do when they are very sad?
97366.e: Crying is a natural reaction to sadness. Afterwards you often feel a bit lighter.
97366.m: When you are sad, you sometimes cry.

97367.e: A pet is a friend. When it dies, you miss it a lot.
97367.m: The death of a pet makes you sad.

97368.q: What do the corners of the mouth look like when someone is sad?
a: They are pulled to the side
97368.e: When you are sad, the corners of your mouth drop. Often the eyes look down too.
97368.m: When you are sad, the corners of your mouth droop.

97369.q: What often helps when a friend is sad?
97369.e: A hug says: I'm here for you. That does sad people good.
97369.m: A hug does sad people good.

97370.q: What flows from your eyes when you cry?
97370.e: When you cry, the eye makes a lot of fluid. These drops are called tears.

97371.q: What is the sad feeling called when you miss your family while away at camp?
97371.e: When you are far from home, you sometimes long for your family. This feeling is called homesickness.
97371.m: If you miss home, you are homesick.

97372.q: What is usually true about sadness?
a: It is catching like a cold
97372.e: Feelings come and go. Even great sadness gets smaller with time.

97373.q: What is the sadness called when a loved one has died?
97373.e: When someone you love dies, you feel grief. Grieving helps you cope with the loss.
97373.m: We grieve for people who have died.

97374.q: Which word describes a sad person?
97374.e: Downcast means sad and low. Lively, jolly and merry describe a good mood.

a: Being able to run very fast
97375.e: Compassion means putting yourself in someone else's shoes. Then you notice whether they are feeling good or bad.
97375.m: Compassion means sensing other people's feelings.

97376.q: A child falls over in the playground and cries. What shows compassion?
a: Asking if they are all right
97376.e: If you ask and help, you show that you care about the other child.

97377.q: What is the word for being able to understand and share other people's feelings?
97377.e: Empathy means that you can understand other people's feelings and feel with them.

97378.q: Which animals comfort each other after a fight, as researchers have observed?
97378.e: Among chimpanzees, one animal often hugs another that has lost a fight. Researchers see this as a form of compassion.

97379.q: What do babies often do when another baby nearby is crying?
97379.e: Even babies react to others crying. They often start crying themselves.
97379.m: Even babies cry when others cry.

97380.q: A new child doesn't know anyone in the class yet. What is a kind thing to do?
97380.e: Being new is often hard. An invitation to play helps them feel at home.

97381.e: With this sentence you show that you take the other person's worries seriously.

97382.q: Without words, what is the best way to tell how someone is feeling?
97382.e: The face gives away a lot about feelings. That is why people like to look at each other when they talk.
97382.m: You can often see feelings in the face.

97383.q: What often happens when everyone near you is laughing loudly?
97383.e: Laughter is catching. When you hear others laughing, you often start laughing yourself.

97384.q: Which animals make sounds when tickled that researchers compare to laughter?
97384.e: Researchers have tickled rats. The animals made very high squeaks that humans cannot hear.
97384.m: Rats react happily to tickling too.

97385.e: On sensitive places like the soles of the feet, tickling makes many people laugh.

97386.q: Why can you hardly tickle yourself?
a: The brain knows what is coming
You only laugh in the evening
97386.e: The brain knows about your own movement in advance. So there is no surprise and no ticklish feeling.

97387.q: At what age do babies usually laugh out loud for the first time?
97387.e: Most babies laugh out loud when they are a few months old. They can smile a little earlier.
97387.m: Babies first laugh out loud at a few months old.

97388.q: What do you call strong laughter that you can't stop?
97388.e: In a fit of laughter you just keep laughing. Sometimes you even cry tears.
97388.m: In a fit of laughter you can't stop laughing.

97389.q: What do you call quiet, secret laughing?
97389.e: When you giggle, you laugh quietly, often behind your hand.

97390.q: How is laughter often written in a comic?
97390.e: In comics and messages, “Haha” stands for laughter. “Atishoo” is a sneeze, “Ouch” is pain.
97390.m: In comics, laughter is written as “Haha”.

97391.q: What often happens when someone next to you yawns?
97391.e: Yawning is catching. When you see someone yawn, you often have to yawn yourself.

97392.q: When do people yawn especially often?
97392.e: Many people yawn before going to sleep and after waking up. Boredom can also make you yawn.

97393.q: Which pet can catch a yawn from humans?
97393.e: Experiments show that dogs sometimes yawn when their human yawns.

97394.q: What is often enough to make you yawn yourself?
97394.e: Just reading or thinking about yawning can set off a yawn. Maybe it's happening to you right now.
97394.m: Even reading about yawning is catching.

97395.q: What do you do with your mouth when you yawn?
97395.e: When you yawn, you open your mouth wide and breathe in deeply.
97395.m: When you yawn, you open your mouth wide.

97396.e: Cats, lions, monkeys and even birds yawn too.

97397.q: Why do you put your hand in front of your mouth when you yawn?
97397.e: An open mouth when yawning is thought to be rude. That is why you put your hand in front of it.
97397.m: When you yawn, put your hand in front of your mouth.

97398.q: According to research, who are you most likely to catch a yawn from?
97398.e: Studies show that yawning is especially catching between people who know each other well.
97398.m: Yawning is especially catching between people who are close.

97399.q: What do you call the way a person shows feelings with their face?
97399.e: With facial expressions you show feelings on your face, for example by smiling or frowning.
97399.m: Feelings on the face are called facial expressions.

97400.q: What do we show with our facial expression?
97400.e: Eyes, mouth and forehead give away whether someone is happy, angry or sad.

97401.q: Which way do your eyebrows move when you are surprised?
97401.e: When you are surprised, you open your eyes wide and raise your eyebrows.
97401.m: When you are surprised, your eyebrows go up.

97402.q: How can you recognise a real, warm smile?
a: By little wrinkles around the eyes
By the tip of the nose
97402.e: With a real smile the eyes smile too. Little wrinkles appear at the corners of the eyes.
97402.m: With a real smile the eyes smile too.

97403.q: What do you often do with your nose when something smells disgusting?
97403.e: When you wrinkle your nose, you scrunch it up. That way you show without words that you find something disgusting.
97403.m: When you are disgusted, you wrinkle your nose.

97404.q: Where do people understand a smile as friendly?
97404.e: A smile is understood as friendly almost everywhere, even if you don't speak the language.
97404.m: A smile is understood almost everywhere in the world.

97405.q: What is it called when you wrinkle your forehead while thinking?
97405.e: When you frown, you pull the skin above your eyes into wrinkles. It shows thinking or annoyance.
97405.m: When you frown, you wrinkle your forehead.

97406.q: What does it often mean when someone winks with one eye?
97406.e: A wink often shows that something is not meant completely seriously.
97406.m: A wink often means it's a joke.

97407.q: What is especially important in a good friendship?
a: You never talk to each other
97407.e: Real friends can rely on each other. They also keep secrets.

97408.q: What do good friends do after an argument?
97408.e: Even friends argue sometimes. Afterwards they say sorry and get on again.
97408.m: Good friends make up after an argument.
